vignette:
Elena sits in the armchair across from my desk, her posture as straight and unyielding as the day she first walked in. At seventy-nine, her hands, resting in her lap, are knotted with arthritis, but they possess a stillness that speaks of immense discipline. These are the same hands, she once told me, that guided a supersonic Mirage jet through the turbulent Andean air, hands that knew the delicate balance between power and control with an intimacy few could ever understand. For forty years, she was a combat pilot for her country’s air force, a pioneer and a patriot. Now, she rarely leaves her daughter’s house.

Her story doesn’t begin in a cockpit, but on a sun-drenched street six months ago. She and her grandson, David, were on their way to the market. He was driving her late husband’s old sedan, a car she kept meticulously maintained. She remembers the scent of jasmine from the neighbor’s yard and the familiar rhythm of the drive. The sudden wail of a siren and the flash of red and blue lights in the rearview mirror were an annoyance, not a threat. David had made an incomplete stop. A simple mistake.

But the two officers who approached the car were not interested in simple mistakes. Their demeanor was aggressive, their questions sharp and accusatory. David, only nineteen, grew flustered, his Spanish faltering. Elena, who had negotiated flight clearances in contested airspace and stared down colonels who believed a woman had no place flying a jet, felt the familiar urge to take command, to de-escalate. She opened her door, intending to speak to the officers calmly, woman to man, elder to youth.

She never got the chance. One of them yelled at her to get back in the car. She remembers raising a hand, palm open, a universal sign for ‘peace’ or ‘wait.’ The officer saw it as defiance. He shoved her. It wasn’t a violent, winding blow, but a short, brutal push to her shoulder. For a woman whose entire career was built on maintaining equilibrium against the pull of gravity, the loss of balance was a profound shock. She fell sideways, her temple and hip striking the pavement with a sickening crack. The world went white, then fuzzy. She recalls the smell of hot asphalt, the rough texture of the concrete against her cheek, and David’s panicked cry. The officers simply stood over her, their faces impassive, before issuing the ticket and leaving.

The bruises on her hip faded within a few weeks. The cut on her temple healed without a scar. But the woman who got up from the pavement was not the same one who had fallen. Elena, who once found solace in the vast, open sky, now feels suffocated by it. Her world has shrunk to the size of her living room. The sound of a passing siren sends a jolt of ice through her veins, her breath catching in her throat as she is slammed back onto the hot asphalt, the officer’s shadow looming over her. She has stopped going for her morning walks to the *panadería*; the sight of a police cruiser a block away is enough to make her turn back, her heart hammering against her ribs.

She sleeps in fits, waking up drenched in sweat from nightmares where she is not in her bed, but pinned under the wreckage of a plane, unable to move. During the day, a relentless vigilance has taken hold. A car door slamming down the street causes her to flinch. She finds herself constantly scanning rooms, noting exits, assessing people, a distorted version of the situational awareness that once kept her alive at 20,000 feet.

Her daughter says she has become a ghost in her own life. The pride she once took in her past is now a source of profound, silent shame. “I faced down enemy fire,” she whispered in our last session, her gaze fixed on a point beyond the window. “I could handle G-force that would make a young man black out. But I was brought down on a sidewalk. By a simple push.” She feels a deep, corrosive guilt, believing she somehow failed her grandson, that her weakness endangered him. The woman who commanded the sky now feels utterly, terrifyingly powerless on the ground.
